     I. INTRODUCTION.

       This is a compelling routing case because every available route carries real impacts. The

record reflects sincere concerns about homes, ranches, wildlife habitat, cultural resources, costs,

community values, and the future use of land that families and communities care deeply about.

Those concerns deserve careful consideration after which time the Commission must apply the

governing standard: select the route that best meets the applicable routing criteria.

       Here, that route is Route 894.1

       The issue before the Commission is not whether Route 894 is perfect. No route of this scale

could be. The question is whether Route 894 (Applicants’ Best Meets Route), Route 572, Cherokee

Creek G (“CCG”), or another alternative route best satisfies the routing criteria when evaluated as

a complete route from end to end. This brief focuses principally on Routes 894, 572, and CCG2

because they share several common links and impacts at the far eastern and western ends of the

study area, making their points of divergence especially important to the Commission’s route-wide

comparison.3

F34, those routes are unlikely to remain serious alternatives in light of recent evidence identifying

        Opponents of Route 894 seek to frame the routing dispute around where the Project should

cross the Colorado River. But that is not the legal standard, and it is not how transmission-line

routes are evaluated. The routing decision must be made on a route-wide basis, not through an

isolated single-link analysis. Focusing only on the Colorado River crossing would distort the

broader comparison the Commission is required to make.

        The noncommon links among Routes 894, 572, and CCG show why that broader

comparison matters. Traveling east to west, the routes diverge well before the Colorado River,

beginning with the routing choice after Link G13. From there, Routes 572 and CCG move

southwest toward links that would affect established homesites, historic ranching operations,

multiple recorded cultural-resource trinomials, including the 600-acre Rose Ranch trinomial,

documented golden-cheeked warbler habitat, and a wider Colorado River crossing at Link J31.

        The western portion of the study area after the Colorado River is equally important. The

testimony of former PUC Commissioner Will McAdams, former PUC Chairman Arthur

D’Andrea, Mark Anderson, Jason Buntz, and others, taken together, addresses the Colorado River

crossing, the San Saba River crossing, cost, environmental impacts, grid reliability and resiliency,

and the head-to-head comparison among Routes 894, 572, and CCG. Their testimony reinforces

the same point reflected throughout the record: when the routes are compared from end to end,

Route 894 provides the better route-wide balance.4

A.      Community values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A).

        PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A) requires consideration of the values and resources essential to a

local community.       Kimley-Horn and Halff, on behalf of Applicants, hosted three public

participation meetings to identify community values.6 These values included habitable structures;

ranching operations; aesthetics; property values; AM/FM, microwave, and other electronic

installations; airstrips and heliports; irrigated pastures or cropland utilizing center-pivot or other

traveling irrigation systems; environmental concerns; existing transmission lines; health concerns;

fish and wildlife; historic resources; and flood protection. Applicants also considered comments

and other information received from governmental agencies, community leaders and the public.7

       1.      Aesthetics.

       Aesthetics addresses the subjective perception of natural beauty in a landscape. 20 This

evaluation attempts to define and evaluate the study area's scenic qualities. Applicants considered

several aesthetic parameters including topography, prominence of water in the landscape,

vegetation variety, diversity of scenic elements, degree of human alteration, and overall uniqueness

scenic views, scenic roadways, scenic drives, or unique visual elements were identified.22 No wild

or scenic rivers, historic trails, national parks, national monuments or national battlefields were

identified either.23 Applicants concluded that the study area comprises a diverse range of land uses,

each of which is influenced by a mix of terrain, waterways, and vegetation.24

that process, TPWD generally recommended avoiding TPWD-managed properties with at least a

0.25-mile buffer from the park boundary; coordinating with TPWD regarding expansion of that

       Applicants used the proper routing framework when selecting Route 894 which uses Link

J22. The filed routes included six viable Colorado River crossing links. Moving generally from

north to south, those options include U3 and U2 to the north, followed by J11, J26, J22, and J31.33

The existence of these six alternatives is important because the record does not support treating

TPWD’s five-mile recommendation as a categorical exclusion of every crossing in the vicinity of

Colorado Bend State Park or Post Oak Ridge State Park. If that were the rule, the route universe

would be severely narrowed by a single resource-agency recommendation rather than by the

Commission’s required route-wide balancing analysis.

record reflects sincere concerns about homes, ranches, wildlife habitat, cultural resources, costs,

a complete route from end to end. This brief focuses principally on Routes 894,572, and CCG~

because they share several common links and impacts at the far eastern and western ends of the

study area, making their points of divergence especially important to the Commission' s route-wide

comparison.3
